read: partial: abstract and sections 1-6 (introduction, related work, construction, MARJ, experiments, analysis, conclusion; pp. 1-9) and appendices A-B (pp. 14-17) read in full; Tables 13-14 (pp. 19-20) and the remaining appendix tables and case studies skimmed; references consulted only for the SciBench entry (p. 12)
venue_now: ICML 2025 (PMLR 267): page 1 footer of arXiv v4, 3 Jun 2025
what_it_is: UGPhysics is a bilingual benchmark of 5,520 undergraduate physics problems (11,040 counting the English translations) across 3 domains, 13 subjects and 59 topics. The problems come from seven Chinese undergraduate physics exercise books, OCR'd with Mathpix and corrected by hand (pp. 1-2, 4). Each problem keeps its reference solution and has one of seven answer types (numerical value, expression, equation, interval, true/false, multiple choice, compound), and GPT-4o labels each with one of four reasoning skills: Knowledge Recall, Laws Application, Math Derivation, Practical Application (p. 4). Answers are scored by MARJ: rule-based matching first, then a GPT-4o judge on items the rules reject (p. 5). Of the 31 LLMs evaluated, the best (OpenAI-o1-mini) reaches 49.8% overall, and math-specialised models gain little over their general counterparts (pp. 1, 6).
domain: undergraduate physics (mechanics and thermodynamics, electromagnetism, modern physics; 13 subjects), in English and Chinese
size: 5,520 problems (11,040 counting both languages), 13 subjects, 59 topics, 7 answer types; 31 LLMs evaluated (pp. 1-2, 4-5)
source_of_items: textbooks: seven undergraduate physics exercise books ('The Great Compendium of Physics Problems', USTC), OCR'd and manually corrected. Progressive problems were split into independent ones; estimation, proof and explanation problems and problems with images were excluded. The originals are Chinese, translated to English (p. 4)
has_gold_traces: partial: every problem keeps the exercise book's reference solution in a Problem-Solution-Answer format (average 318.5 solution tokens, Table 2, p. 4), but scoring uses only the final answer (p. 5)
evaluation: final answer: MARJ, a rule-based stage followed by a GPT-4o judge on the cases the rules mark False. In the rule stage, numerical answers are compared on the base of their scientific notation only, within 1e-2 relative error; expressions and equations are normalised by removing physical constants; SymPy checks equivalence (p. 5; App. B.4, pp. 16-17)
human_validation: The authors' team manually reviewed and corrected the OCR output and LaTeX (p. 4). MARJ agreed with human correctness annotations on 98% of 100 randomly selected test examples (section 5.2, p. 7). Human evaluators annotated 100 incorrect o1-mini answers for error type (p. 8). No human check of the GPT-4o skill labels is reported (p. 4; App. A.3, p. 14).
contamination_measures: embedding-based deduplication (p. 4); n-gram (5-gram) leakage detection on 8 open models: 0.0% to 0.75% of samples flagged as contaminated, 0.0% to 0.68% both contaminated and answered correctly (section 5.4 and Table 6, pp. 8-9)

engtrace_use.sentence: S-P1 (L172-177): 'While UGPhysics (Xu et al., 2025) and PhysReason (Zhang et al., 2025a) effectively test the application of reasoning to natural laws, others target advanced symbolic (...) or qualitative (...) understanding.' S-P2 (L177-180, no citation, covers all six): 'Despite this progress, these benchmarks remain confined to theoretical physics, lacking the integrative context of engineering.'
engtrace_use.explanation: S-P1 holds in gist: UGPhysics tests undergraduate physics problem solving that needs laws and principles (p. 2), and Laws Application is one of its four skill labels (p. 4). But S-P1's split between benchmarks that test 'the application of reasoning to natural laws' and those that 'target advanced symbolic' understanding does not fit this paper. Its largest skill category is Math Derivation (4,440 of 11,040 items, against 3,914 for Laws Application; Table 14, p. 20), and two of its answer types are expressions and equations (Table 3, p. 4). S-P2 is loose: UGPhysics covers undergraduate coursework in 13 subjects, including semiconductor and solid-state physics, optics, and a Practical Application skill (1,106 of 11,040 items; Tables 13-14, pp. 19-20). That is not theoretical physics in the subfield sense, though 'not engineering' is right. The section also leaves out what matters for EngTrace's comparison: UGPhysics scores only final answers, partly with an LLM judge (p. 5).

suggested_wording: UGPhysics (Xu et al., 2025) collects 5,520 undergraduate physics problems from exercise books, in English and Chinese, and scores only the final answer, with rule-based matching backed by a GPT-4o judge.
facts_to_cite: 5,520 undergraduate-level physics problems in English and Chinese (11,040 in total), 13 subjects, 59 topics, seven answer types (pp. 1-2, 4)
the problems come from seven undergraduate physics exercise books, OCR'd and manually corrected (p. 4)
answers are judged by MARJ: rule-based matching, then GPT-4o on the cases the rules reject (p. 5); MARJ agreed with human judgement on 98% of 100 sampled examples (p. 7)
data leakage was screened with 5-gram accuracy; no tested model had more than 0.75% of samples flagged (pp. 8-9)
of 31 LLMs evaluated, the best overall accuracy is 49.8% (OpenAI-o1-mini) (p. 1)
math-specialised LLMs improve only slightly over their general-purpose counterparts: Qwen2.5-Math gains 0.14 points at 7B and 3.3 at 72B (p. 6)
overlap_with_engtrace: Shares: multi-step quantitative science problems with exact reference answers; a tolerance-based numeric answer check (1e-2 relative on the mantissa, against EngTrace's REL 0.002); reference solutions; a leakage check; a small human check of the answer evaluator (98% on 100). Lacks: generated instances (its exercise-book problems are static); gold traces used in scoring, and any step-level evaluation (it scores the final answer only); the engineering domain (it is physics coursework, though a few topics such as circuit analysis and fluid mechanics border engineering science, Table 13, p. 19); expert validation of the evaluator beyond the authors' 100-item check; a deterministic-only answer check (its second stage is a GPT-4o judge).
notes: Its finding that math-specialised models gain little on physics (p. 6) bears on the math-pretraining claim EngTrace has dropped (state brief, section 5); do not cite it in support of a claim EngTrace no longer makes. The numeric rule compares only the base of the scientific notation (p. 5), so it ignores the power of ten; keep this in mind if tolerances are compared. UGPhysics itself cites SciBench as a prior college-level science benchmark (p. 2; reference list p. 12). The May reference list gets 8 of 9 first names wrong. The paper (p. 1) has Xin Xu, Qiyun Xu, Tong Xiao, Tianhao Chen, Yuchen Yan, Jiaxin Zhang, Shizhe Diao, Can Yang, Yang Wang; the key is unaffected.
